Elusive

/ih-LOO-siv/ — rhymes with "exclusive" · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something elusive is difficult to find, catch, or pin down.

The elusive snow leopard was photographed only twice in ten years.

Worked Example

A detective chased a suspect who vanished at every checkpoint, always staying one step ahead of capture.

Elusive is more precise than "hard to find" because it captures not just difficulty but a pattern of slipping away—the sense that the target actively evades capture. This is exactly what the detective experiences.

How Elusive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

evasive

evasive: skillfully dodging capture or direct questions

fleeting

fleeting: vanishing almost as soon as it appears

mysterious

mysterious: puzzling because it stays out of reach

Antonyms

obvious

obvious: impossible to miss or mistake

conspicuous

conspicuous: standing out where everyone can see

How Strong Is It? — uncommon → hard to find → impossible to locate → elusive

uncommon vs. elusive

uncommon vs. elusive: Uncommon is much weaker than elusive — an uncommon bird is simply rare, while an elusive one seems to slip away whenever you get close.

hard to find vs. elusive

hard to find vs. elusive: 'Hard to find' is a step below elusive: a hard-to-find book takes patience to track down, but an elusive one appears to dodge every search.

impossible to locate vs. elusive

impossible to locate vs. elusive: 'Impossible to locate' goes beyond elusive — an elusive fox can still occasionally be caught, while something impossible to locate never turns up at all.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of elusive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out, away (form of ex-) (Latin)

Root — lus

Root — lus: to play (from ludere) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to, inclined to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: E- ('out, away') + lus ('to play') + -ive ('tending to') builds 'tending to play its way out' — an elusive thing playfully slips away from anyone trying to catch it or pin it down.

Use the root in a new word: interlude

Use the root in a new word: interlude: An interlude was originally a short play performed between the acts of a drama — the same Latin ludere, 'to play,' that lets an elusive thing play hide-and-seek with whoever is chasing it.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Use elusive when something is inherently difficult to find, catch, or pin down—often applied to rare animals, fleeting feelings, or hard-to-define ideas. For someone avoiding you on purpose, say "evasive." For something that simply doesn't exist or isn't available, say "hard to find."
